description: Break a problem down to its fundamental truths and reason upward from there instead of by analogy. State the problem with no solution baked in, enumerate every assumption, separate real constraints from inherited conventions, discard the conventions, rebuild a solution from the hard constraints, and validate it. Reasoning from first principles finds options that copying the industry template hides.

steps.description: State the problem precisely and strip out any assumed solution. Most problem statements smuggle in a preferred answer, which blocks original thinking before it starts.

inputs.name: problem-description
inputs.desc: The problem or goal, in the user's own words

inputs.name: current-approach
inputs.desc: How the problem is handled today, or the default industry approach

inputs.name: desired-outcome
inputs.desc: What a good result would actually look like

outputs.name: problem-statement
outputs.desc: The problem restated with no solution assumed

outputs.name: solution-free-framing
outputs.desc: The core need expressed as a requirement, not a method

process: Write the problem in one or two plain sentences a non-expert could follow.
Underline every word that names a specific solution or method rather than a need.
Rewrite the statement so it describes the need and the desired outcome only, with no method implied.
Confirm the restated problem still captures the real goal and nothing has been narrowed away.

steps.description: List every assumption baked into the current approach. You cannot question an assumption you have not named, so the goal here is completeness, not judgment.

inputs.name: problem-statement
inputs.desc: The problem restated with no solution assumed

inputs.name: solution-free-framing
inputs.desc: The core need expressed as a requirement

outputs.name: assumption-list
outputs.desc: Every assumption behind the current approach, one per line

outputs.name: assumption-count
outputs.desc: How many distinct assumptions were surfaced

process: For the current approach, ask what has to be true for this to make sense and write each answer down.
Cover cost, time, materials, rules, customer behavior, and technical limits. Each is a source of hidden assumptions.
Phrase each assumption as a claim that could be true or false, not as a vague worry.
Do not judge any assumption yet. Capture first, test later.
Count the distinct assumptions so the next step has a clear list to work through.

steps.description: Sort each assumption into a fundamental truth or an inherited convention. A fundamental truth is required by a law of physics, math, or economics. A convention is just how things have been done.

inputs.name: assumption-list
inputs.desc: Every assumption behind the current approach

inputs.name: assumption-count
inputs.desc: How many distinct assumptions were surfaced

outputs.name: classified-assumptions
outputs.desc: Each assumption tagged as fundamental truth or convention, with a one-line reason

outputs.name: convention-list
outputs.desc: The subset of assumptions that are only convention

process: For each assumption, ask whether it is required by a physical, mathematical, or economic law, or is just customary.
Tag it as a fundamental truth only if breaking it breaks a real law. Otherwise tag it convention.
Write a one-line reason for each tag so the call can be checked later.
Collect every convention into a separate list. These are the candidates for removal.

steps.description: Challenge and discard the conventions. For each one, ask what the world would actually allow if the convention did not exist, and keep only the hard constraints that remain.

inputs.name: convention-list
inputs.desc: The assumptions that are only convention

inputs.name: classified-assumptions
inputs.desc: Each assumption tagged fundamental truth or convention

outputs.name: hard-constraints
outputs.desc: The real limits that survive scrutiny

outputs.name: discarded-conventions
outputs.desc: The conventions dropped, with what each one was costing

process: Take each convention and ask, if nobody did it this way, what would actually stop us.
If the honest answer is nothing but habit or industry norm, discard the convention.
Record what each discarded convention was costing in time, money, or options.
Combine the surviving fundamental truths into a clean list of hard constraints.

steps.description: Rebuild a solution from the hard constraints upward, reasoning from the fundamentals rather than copying how others solved it. The constraints define the smallest box the answer must fit.

inputs.name: hard-constraints
inputs.desc: The real limits that survive scrutiny

inputs.name: discarded-conventions
inputs.desc: The conventions dropped and what they cost

outputs.name: first-principles-solution
outputs.desc: A solution derived from the constraints, not from analogy

outputs.name: reasoning-trace
outputs.desc: The step-by-step derivation from each constraint to the solution

process: Start from the hard constraints and nothing else. Treat the discarded conventions as freed-up room, not rules.
Ask what the cheapest or simplest thing is that satisfies every hard constraint.
Build the solution one constraint at a time, writing down why each design choice follows from a constraint.
Resist reaching for how the industry does it. If a choice is there only because others do it, mark it for review.
Keep the reasoning trace so anyone can follow each step from constraint to conclusion.

steps.description: Validate the rebuilt solution against the original problem and the hard constraints. A first-principles solution is only useful if it still solves the real need and breaks no genuine limit.

inputs.name: first-principles-solution
inputs.desc: A solution derived from the constraints

inputs.name: hard-constraints
inputs.desc: The real limits that survive scrutiny

inputs.name: problem-statement
inputs.desc: The problem restated with no solution assumed

outputs.name: validated-solution
outputs.desc: The solution after checking it against the problem and constraints

outputs.name: open-questions
outputs.desc: Risks and unknowns that need testing before committing

process: Check the solution against the original problem statement. Does it meet the real need, not a narrowed version?
Check it against every hard constraint. Any break sends you back to the rebuild step.
List the assumptions in the new solution that are still untested, and how you would test each one.
State the open questions plainly so the solution is not mistaken for proven before it is.

description: Assess a business for a durable competitive moat using the four moat types: cost advantages, switching costs, network effects, and intangible assets. Score each type honestly with evidence, synthesize a scorecard, and reach a verdict. A business with no real moat competes on execution alone, which a better-resourced rival can eventually win.

steps.description: Capture the business model, customers, and competitors so the moat assessment has concrete facts to work from. Vague inputs produce flattering, useless moat scores.

inputs.name: business-description
inputs.desc: What the business sells and how it makes money

inputs.name: customer-base
inputs.desc: Who the customers are and why they buy

inputs.name: main-competitors
inputs.desc: The rivals who could take this business

outputs.name: business-profile
outputs.desc: A tight profile of the business model and customers

outputs.name: competitor-set
outputs.desc: The named set of real competitors

process: Write how the business makes money in two or three sentences.
Describe who buys, how often, and what they would use instead.
Name the real competitors, including the next-best alternative a customer could switch to.
Keep the profile factual. Save judgments about strength for the scoring steps.

steps.description: Assess whether the business has a durable cost advantage: the ability to produce or deliver at lower cost than rivals in a way they cannot easily copy. Scale, process, location, and privileged access are the usual sources.

inputs.name: business-profile
inputs.desc: A tight profile of the business model and customers

inputs.name: competitor-set
inputs.desc: The named set of real competitors

outputs.name: cost-advantage-score
outputs.desc: A 0 to 5 score for durable cost advantage

outputs.name: cost-advantage-evidence
outputs.desc: The concrete reasons behind the score

process: Ask whether the business can deliver the same thing at lower cost than the competitor set, and why.
Trace the cost edge to a source: scale, a better process, a location, or privileged access to inputs.
Test durability. If a well-funded rival could match the cost in a year, the advantage is weak.
Score 0 to 5 and write the evidence. A score with no evidence is a guess.

steps.description: Assess switching costs: how much time, money, or risk a customer takes on to leave for a competitor. High switching costs keep customers even when a rival is slightly better or cheaper.

inputs.name: business-profile
inputs.desc: A tight profile of the business model and customers

inputs.name: competitor-set
inputs.desc: The named set of real competitors

outputs.name: switching-cost-score
outputs.desc: A 0 to 5 score for customer switching cost

outputs.name: switching-cost-evidence
outputs.desc: What specifically makes leaving costly

process: Walk through what a customer must do to move to a competitor: data, retraining, contracts, integration, risk.
Estimate the real cost of each in time, money, and risk to the customer.
Ask whether the switching cost is rising or falling as the market matures.
Score 0 to 5 and record the specific sources of the cost.

steps.description: Assess network effects: whether the product becomes more valuable to each user as more users join. Strong network effects make the leading product hard to displace because value, not just size, grows with scale.

inputs.name: business-profile
inputs.desc: A tight profile of the business model and customers

inputs.name: competitor-set
inputs.desc: The named set of real competitors

outputs.name: network-effect-score
outputs.desc: A 0 to 5 score for network effect strength

outputs.name: network-effect-evidence
outputs.desc: The user-to-user value that grows with scale

process: Ask whether one more user makes the product better for existing users, and how.
Name the interaction that creates the effect: more buyers draw more sellers, more users create more data, and so on.
Check whether the effect is local or global. Local effects can be beaten market by market.
Score 0 to 5 and write down the specific value that grows with user count.

steps.description: Assess intangible assets: brand, patents, licenses, regulatory approvals, and culture that rivals cannot simply buy or copy. These assets protect pricing and keep customers choosing the business by default.

inputs.name: business-profile
inputs.desc: A tight profile of the business model and customers

inputs.name: competitor-set
inputs.desc: The named set of real competitors

outputs.name: intangible-asset-score
outputs.desc: A 0 to 5 score for intangible asset strength

outputs.name: intangible-asset-evidence
outputs.desc: The specific protected assets and what they shield

process: List intangible assets: brand trust, patents, exclusive licenses, regulatory approvals, and hard-to-copy culture.
For each, ask what it protects: price, default choice, or access to a restricted market.
Test whether a rival could buy or rebuild the asset, and how long that would take.
Score 0 to 5 and name the assets behind the score.

steps.description: Combine the four moat scores into a single honest scorecard. The point is to see which moats are real, which are wishful, and whether any one of them is strong enough to rely on.

inputs.name: cost-advantage-score
inputs.desc: A 0 to 5 score for durable cost advantage

inputs.name: switching-cost-score
inputs.desc: A 0 to 5 score for customer switching cost

inputs.name: network-effect-score
inputs.desc: A 0 to 5 score for network effect strength

inputs.name: intangible-asset-score
inputs.desc: A 0 to 5 score for intangible asset strength

outputs.name: moat-scorecard
outputs.desc: The four scores side by side with their evidence

outputs.name: dominant-moat
outputs.desc: The strongest moat, or a note that none is strong

process: Place the four scores side by side with their evidence lines.
Flag any score above 3 as a candidate real moat and any at or below 1 as absent.
Identify the dominant moat, the single strongest and most durable one.
If no score clears 3, state plainly that there is no strong moat yet.

steps.description: Reach a verdict: does this business have a real moat, or is it competing on execution alone? Name what to build or deepen so the business is not left defending a position any better-resourced rival can take.

inputs.name: moat-scorecard
inputs.desc: The four scores side by side with their evidence

inputs.name: dominant-moat
inputs.desc: The strongest moat, or a note that none is strong

outputs.name: moat-verdict
outputs.desc: A clear statement of whether a durable moat exists

outputs.name: moat-building-priorities
outputs.desc: The ranked moves to build or widen a moat

process: State the verdict in one line: durable moat, partial moat, or execution-only.
If execution-only, say so plainly. Competing on execution means a better-funded rival can eventually win.
Pick the one or two moat types with the best chance of becoming durable for this business.
List the specific moves to build or widen those moats, ranked by payoff.

description: Find uncontested market space with the four actions framework from blue ocean strategy. List the factors the industry competes on, then decide which to eliminate, which to reduce, which to raise, and which to create. The combination defines a new value curve that steps out of the crowded red ocean.

steps.description: Map the factors the whole industry competes on and where the current offering sits on each. This is the starting value curve, the shape you are trying to change.

inputs.name: industry-description
inputs.desc: The industry and how it competes today

inputs.name: current-offering
inputs.desc: The product or service as it stands now

inputs.name: target-customer
inputs.desc: Who the offering is for, including non-customers worth reaching

outputs.name: competition-factors
outputs.desc: The factors the industry competes on, one per line

outputs.name: current-factor-levels
outputs.desc: Where today's offering sits on each factor, high, medium, or low

process: List every factor the industry sells on: price, features, service levels, convenience, and so on.
For each factor, mark where the current offering sits: high, medium, or low.
Include factors customers quietly dislike but the industry provides anyway.
This set of factors and levels is the current value curve. Name it as the baseline.

steps.description: Decide which factors the industry takes for granted can be eliminated entirely. Removing a factor nobody truly values frees cost and often reveals that a long-assumed requirement was never needed.

inputs.name: competition-factors
inputs.desc: The factors the industry competes on

inputs.name: current-factor-levels
inputs.desc: Where today's offering sits on each factor

outputs.name: eliminate-list
outputs.desc: Factors to remove entirely

outputs.name: eliminate-rationale
outputs.desc: Why each one can go and what it frees

process: For each factor, ask whether the customer truly values it or the industry provides it out of habit.
Mark for elimination any factor that exists mainly because competitors all have it.
For each elimination, note the cost or complexity it removes.
Be willing to remove a factor the industry considers essential if customers do not value it.

steps.description: Decide which factors can be reduced well below the industry standard. Industries often overserve on factors in a race to match rivals, loading cost onto things customers do not need that much of.

inputs.name: competition-factors
inputs.desc: The factors the industry competes on

inputs.name: eliminate-list
inputs.desc: Factors already marked for removal

outputs.name: reduce-list
outputs.desc: Factors to dial well below industry norm

outputs.name: reduce-rationale
outputs.desc: Why over-serving on each one wastes cost

process: Look at the factors that survived elimination and ask which are overserved.
Find factors the industry escalates to beat rivals past the point customers care about.
Mark those to reduce well below the standard, and say how far.
Record the cost that the reduction frees for use elsewhere.

steps.description: Decide which factors should be raised well above the industry standard. These are the points where customers are underserved and would value much more than the industry currently offers.

inputs.name: competition-factors
inputs.desc: The factors the industry competes on

inputs.name: reduce-list
inputs.desc: Factors already marked to reduce

outputs.name: raise-list
outputs.desc: Factors to push well above industry norm

outputs.name: raise-rationale
outputs.desc: The underserved need each one answers

process: Find the factors where customers settle for less than they want because the whole industry underdelivers.
Mark those to raise well above the standard, and say how far.
Tie each raise to a specific unmet need or recurring customer complaint.
Check that the raises are funded by the cost freed from the eliminate and reduce passes.

steps.description: Decide which brand-new factors to create that the industry has never offered. Created factors are the main source of new demand, because they answer needs the industry taught customers to stop expecting.

inputs.name: competition-factors
inputs.desc: The factors the industry competes on

inputs.name: raise-list
inputs.desc: Factors already marked to raise

outputs.name: create-list
outputs.desc: New factors the industry never offered

outputs.name: create-rationale
outputs.desc: The new demand each one opens

process: Ask what customers work around, tolerate, or go elsewhere for because the industry never addressed it.
Look at non-customers: what keeps them out of the market entirely?
Define new factors that answer those needs and have no equivalent in the current value curve.
For each new factor, name the new demand or new buyer it could bring in.

steps.description: Combine the four passes into a new value curve and define the uncontested space it opens. A strong new curve looks clearly different from the industry baseline, not like a slightly tuned copy.

inputs.name: eliminate-list
inputs.desc: Factors to remove entirely

inputs.name: reduce-list
inputs.desc: Factors to dial well below industry norm

inputs.name: raise-list
inputs.desc: Factors to push well above industry norm

inputs.name: create-list
inputs.desc: New factors the industry never offered

outputs.name: value-curve
outputs.desc: The new value curve after all four actions

outputs.name: uncontested-space-definition
outputs.desc: The market space the new curve claims and who it serves

process: Redraw the value curve applying all four actions: eliminate, reduce, raise, create.
Compare it to the industry baseline. A curve that tracks the baseline has not escaped the red ocean.
State the uncontested space the new curve claims and the customers, including former non-customers, it serves.
Confirm the lower-cost moves fund the higher-value moves so the position is sustainable.

description: Apply John Boyd's OODA loop (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act) to a competitive situation where speed of decision matters. Map each stage of your loop, measure its latency, find the slowest stage, and shrink it. The side that cycles faster acts on newer information while rivals react to moves already changed.

steps.description: Capture the competitive situation and the decisions being made over and over. The OODA loop applies where the same kind of decision repeats against a reacting opponent, so name that loop clearly.

inputs.name: situation-description
inputs.desc: The competitive situation and who you are up against

inputs.name: decision-cadence
inputs.desc: How often the key decisions repeat

inputs.name: competitor-tempo
inputs.desc: How fast rivals seem to respond

outputs.name: loop-context
outputs.desc: The situation framed as a repeating decision loop

outputs.name: decision-inventory
outputs.desc: The specific recurring decisions in the loop

process: Describe the situation as a loop: a decision made, acted on, observed, and made again.
List the recurring decisions that make up the loop.
Note how fast rivals react, since the advantage is relative loop speed, not absolute speed.
Confirm the situation really is a repeating loop against a reacting opponent, not a one-time choice.

steps.description: Map the Observe stage: how raw information about the situation reaches you and how long that takes. Stale or slow observation starts the whole loop behind.

inputs.name: loop-context
inputs.desc: The situation framed as a repeating decision loop

inputs.name: decision-inventory
inputs.desc: The specific recurring decisions in the loop

outputs.name: observe-map
outputs.desc: How information is gathered and from where

outputs.name: observe-latency
outputs.desc: The time from an event to you knowing about it

process: Trace how you learn what is happening: sensors, reports, dashboards, customer signals.
Measure the delay from an event occurring to you first seeing it.
Flag blind spots, the events you do not observe at all.
Record the observe latency as a number so stages can be compared later.

steps.description: Map the Orient stage: how raw information becomes understanding you can act on. Boyd called Orient the most important stage, and it is usually where the loop slows down.

inputs.name: loop-context
inputs.desc: The situation framed as a repeating decision loop

inputs.name: observe-map
inputs.desc: How information is gathered and from where

outputs.name: orient-map
outputs.desc: How information is turned into meaning and options

outputs.name: orient-latency
outputs.desc: The time from seeing information to understanding what it means

process: Trace how observations are interpreted: analysis, mental models, past experience, team discussion.
Measure the delay from seeing information to understanding what it means for the decision.
Find where orientation stalls: too much data, wrong mental models, or waiting on one expert.
Record the orient latency as a number.

steps.description: Map the Decide stage: how an understanding turns into a chosen action, including every approval the decision must pass through. Decision rights and sign-offs are common hidden delays here.

inputs.name: loop-context
inputs.desc: The situation framed as a repeating decision loop

inputs.name: orient-map
inputs.desc: How information is turned into meaning and options

outputs.name: decide-map
outputs.desc: How decisions get made and who must approve them

outputs.name: decide-latency
outputs.desc: The time from understanding to a committed choice

process: Trace how a choice gets made: who decides, who must approve, and what evidence they require.
Measure the delay from having understanding to a committed decision.
Flag every approval step and ask whether it adds judgment or only adds delay.
Record the decide latency as a number.

steps.description: Map the Act stage: how a decision becomes a real action the opponent can observe. A fast decision that executes slowly still hands the opponent time to react.

inputs.name: loop-context
inputs.desc: The situation framed as a repeating decision loop

inputs.name: decide-map
inputs.desc: How decisions get made and who must approve them

outputs.name: act-map
outputs.desc: How decisions turn into executed actions

outputs.name: act-latency
outputs.desc: The time from a decision to action in the world

process: Trace how a decision becomes action: handoffs, build time, deployment, communication.
Measure the delay from decision to the action being real and visible.
Flag handoffs where a decision waits in a queue before anyone acts.
Record the act latency as a number.

steps.description: Add the four stage latencies into total cycle time and find the slowest stage. The bottleneck is the single stage that costs the most time, and it is the only stage worth attacking first.

inputs.name: observe-latency
inputs.desc: The time from an event to you knowing about it

inputs.name: orient-latency
inputs.desc: The time from seeing information to understanding it

inputs.name: decide-latency
inputs.desc: The time from understanding to a committed choice

inputs.name: act-latency
inputs.desc: The time from a decision to action in the world

outputs.name: loop-bottleneck
outputs.desc: The slowest stage and its share of total cycle time

outputs.name: cycle-time-total
outputs.desc: The full loop time from event to action

process: Add the four latencies to get the total cycle time.
Rank the stages by how much time each one costs.
Name the slowest stage as the bottleneck and give its share of the total.
Compare total cycle time to the competitor tempo. Slower than the rival means you react to old moves.

steps.description: Design changes to shrink the bottleneck and speed the whole loop. Faster cycling lets you act on newer information and forces the opponent to keep reacting to moves you have already changed.

inputs.name: loop-bottleneck
inputs.desc: The slowest stage and its share of total cycle time

inputs.name: cycle-time-total
inputs.desc: The full loop time from event to action

outputs.name: compression-plan
outputs.desc: Specific changes to cut the bottleneck stage

outputs.name: target-cycle-time
outputs.desc: The cycle time you aim for and why it beats the rival

process: Attack the bottleneck first. Speeding any other stage barely moves the total.
List specific changes: remove an approval, pre-decide common cases, automate a handoff, cut a data source.
Set a target cycle time that is faster than the competitor tempo, not just faster than today.
Plan to re-measure after the change, since the bottleneck usually moves to a new stage.

description: Find an asymmetric advantage by overlapping your real strengths with your competitors' structural weaknesses, then invert to see where to avoid fighting. Competing where you are strong and they are weak lets you play a different game instead of a head-to-head fight you may not win.

steps.description: Capture your business, your resources, and the competitor field so the advantage search rests on facts. Honest inputs matter most here, since the method fails if you overrate yourself or underrate rivals.

inputs.name: your-business-description
inputs.desc: What your business does and how

inputs.name: available-resources
inputs.desc: The people, money, time, and access you actually have

inputs.name: main-competitors
inputs.desc: The rivals you compete with for the same customers

outputs.name: business-context
outputs.desc: A factual profile of your business

outputs.name: competitor-set
outputs.desc: The named competitors

outputs.name: resource-summary
outputs.desc: Your real resources and access

process: Describe your business plainly: what you do and for whom.
List the resources you truly have, not the ones you wish you had.
Name the competitors who go after the same customers.
Keep it factual. Judgments about strength and weakness come in the next steps.

steps.description: Inventory your real strengths and your real weaknesses. Both matter: strengths feed the advantage search and weaknesses mark the zones you must avoid fighting in.

inputs.name: business-context
inputs.desc: A factual profile of your business

inputs.name: resource-summary
inputs.desc: Your real resources and access

outputs.name: strength-list
outputs.desc: Your durable, real strengths

outputs.name: self-weakness-list
outputs.desc: The weaknesses you cannot quickly fix

process: List strengths that are durable and specific, not generic claims like good service.
For each strength, note the evidence that it is real and hard to copy.
List your weaknesses honestly, especially the structural ones you cannot fix soon.
Keep the two lists separate. They are used in different later steps.

steps.description: Map the structural weaknesses of each competitor, the limits built into their size, model, or commitments that they cannot easily escape. Structural weaknesses are more reliable to attack than temporary stumbles.

inputs.name: competitor-set
inputs.desc: The named competitors

inputs.name: business-context
inputs.desc: A factual profile of your business

outputs.name: competitor-weakness-map
outputs.desc: Each competitor's structural weaknesses

outputs.name: competitor-strength-map
outputs.desc: Each competitor's real strengths

process: For each competitor, find weaknesses built into their size, business model, or past commitments.
Separate structural weaknesses, which are hard for them to fix, from temporary ones.
Also record each competitor's genuine strengths, needed for the avoid-zone step.
Favor weaknesses a large rival cannot address without hurting their core business.

steps.description: Overlap your strengths with competitor weaknesses. Where a real strength of yours lines up with a structural weakness of theirs is an asymmetric advantage, a place you can win that they cannot easily contest.

inputs.name: strength-list
inputs.desc: Your durable, real strengths

inputs.name: competitor-weakness-map
inputs.desc: Each competitor's structural weaknesses

outputs.name: asymmetric-advantages
outputs.desc: The overlaps where you are strong and rivals are structurally weak

outputs.name: advantage-ranking
outputs.desc: The overlaps ranked by size and durability

process: Lay your strength list against the competitor weakness map.
Mark every point where a real strength meets a structural weakness of a rival.
Keep only overlaps where the rival cannot copy you without damaging their own model.
Rank the overlaps by how large and how durable the advantage is.

steps.description: Invert the analysis: where your weaknesses meet competitors' strengths are the zones to avoid. Fighting there is a head-to-head battle on their terms, the exact fight an asymmetric strategy exists to skip.

inputs.name: self-weakness-list
inputs.desc: The weaknesses you cannot quickly fix

inputs.name: competitor-strength-map
inputs.desc: Each competitor's real strengths

outputs.name: avoid-zones
outputs.desc: The areas where you are weak and rivals are strong

outputs.name: head-to-head-risks
outputs.desc: The specific fights to refuse

process: Lay your self-weakness list against the competitor strength map.
Mark every point where your weakness meets a rival strength. These are avoid zones.
Name the specific head-to-head fights that would drag you into those zones.
Treat avoid zones as discipline: winning elsewhere means not fighting here.

steps.description: Turn the advantages and avoid zones into a plan to play a different game. The plan concentrates effort where you are asymmetrically strong and steers clear of the fights that favor the competition.

inputs.name: asymmetric-advantages
inputs.desc: The overlaps where you are strong and rivals are structurally weak

inputs.name: avoid-zones
inputs.desc: The areas where you are weak and rivals are strong

outputs.name: positioning-move
outputs.desc: The positioning that leans on your asymmetric advantage

outputs.name: game-plan-summary
outputs.desc: The concrete moves and the fights you will refuse

process: Choose the top-ranked asymmetric advantage as the base of the positioning.
Describe a position that makes your advantage central and the rival's strength beside the point.
Write the concrete moves that build on the advantage and the fights you will refuse.
Check the plan does not quietly drag you back into an avoid zone.

description: Judge whether a market opportunity is too early, too late, or on time using three signals: are people already paying for workarounds, have three or more competitors entered in two years, and is the enabling technology in place and affordable. Timing beats many products, so read the signals before committing.

steps.description: Capture the opportunity and the product idea so the timing signals have something concrete to test. Timing is judged against a specific offering for a specific market, not a vague theme.

inputs.name: opportunity-description
inputs.desc: The problem and the market opportunity

inputs.name: product-idea
inputs.desc: The product or service you would build

inputs.name: target-market
inputs.desc: Who would buy and roughly how many

outputs.name: opportunity-profile
outputs.desc: A tight profile of the opportunity and offering

outputs.name: timing-question-set
outputs.desc: The three timing questions framed for this opportunity

process: State the opportunity: the problem, who has it, and why it matters now.
Describe the product idea you would bring to it.
Frame the three timing questions for this specific case: workarounds, competitor entries, enabling technology.
Keep the profile concrete so each signal can be answered with evidence.

steps.description: Read the first signal: are people already spending time or money on workarounds to this problem? Existing spending on clumsy workarounds is the strongest sign that real demand already exists.

inputs.name: opportunity-profile
inputs.desc: A tight profile of the opportunity and offering

inputs.name: timing-question-set
inputs.desc: The three timing questions framed for this opportunity

outputs.name: workaround-evidence
outputs.desc: Evidence of money or effort spent on workarounds today

outputs.name: demand-signal-strength
outputs.desc: How strong the existing demand looks, low, medium, or high

process: Find how people solve this problem today, including manual, duct-tape, or multi-tool workarounds.
Estimate the time or money they already spend on those workarounds.
Treat spending on a bad workaround as proof of demand. No workaround spending is a warning of too early.
Rate the demand signal low, medium, or high with the evidence behind it.

steps.description: Read the second signal: have three or more competitors entered this space in the last two years? A wave of recent entrants shows the market is waking up. A crowd of long-established players can show you are late.

inputs.name: opportunity-profile
inputs.desc: A tight profile of the opportunity and offering

inputs.name: timing-question-set
inputs.desc: The three timing questions framed for this opportunity

outputs.name: competitor-entry-count
outputs.desc: How many competitors entered in the last two years

outputs.name: entry-trend
outputs.desc: Whether entry is accelerating, steady, or long settled

process: Count the competitors who entered this space in the last two years.
Note whether entry is speeding up, steady, or whether the field settled long ago.
Read three or more recent entrants as a sign the timing window is opening.
Read a long-settled field of entrenched players as a sign you may be late.

steps.description: Read the third signal: is the enabling technology in place and affordable enough to build and deliver the product now? Many good ideas fail only because the technology they need is not ready or not cheap yet.

inputs.name: opportunity-profile
inputs.desc: A tight profile of the opportunity and offering

inputs.name: timing-question-set
inputs.desc: The three timing questions framed for this opportunity

outputs.name: technology-readiness
outputs.desc: Whether the needed technology exists and is reliable

outputs.name: cost-trend
outputs.desc: Whether the cost to build and deliver is falling to a workable level

process: List the technologies the product depends on to work and to scale.
Check whether each one exists today and is reliable enough to build on.
Check whether the cost of those technologies is falling toward a level the market can bear.
Rate technology readiness and note the cost trend with evidence.

steps.description: Combine the three signals into one timing read. The signals can disagree, and the tensions between them are as informative as the signals themselves.

inputs.name: demand-signal-strength
inputs.desc: How strong the existing demand looks

inputs.name: competitor-entry-count
inputs.desc: How many competitors entered in the last two years

inputs.name: technology-readiness
inputs.desc: Whether the needed technology exists and is reliable

outputs.name: timing-signal-summary
outputs.desc: The three signals summarized together

outputs.name: timing-tensions
outputs.desc: Where the signals disagree and what that implies

process: Put the three signals side by side: demand, competitor entry, and technology readiness.
Note where they agree, which strengthens the read.
Note where they disagree, such as strong demand but technology not ready, a classic too-early pattern.
Summarize the combined picture without forcing a verdict yet.

steps.description: Reach a timing verdict: too early, too late, or on time, and state the action it implies. A timing verdict is only useful if it changes what you do next, not just a label.

inputs.name: timing-signal-summary
inputs.desc: The three signals summarized together

inputs.name: timing-tensions
inputs.desc: Where the signals disagree and what that implies

outputs.name: timing-verdict
outputs.desc: Too early, too late, or on time, with the reasoning

outputs.name: timing-action
outputs.desc: What the verdict implies you should do now

process: Weigh the combined signals into one verdict: too early, too late, or on time.
If too early, decide whether to wait, build a bridge product, or shape the market.
If too late, decide whether a differentiated entry is still possible or the window has closed.
If on time, state what moving now requires and what would make you move faster.

description: Build a strategic retreat framework by defining the triggers for pulling back before you are in the situation, so the decision is made with a cool head rather than under sunk-cost pressure. Retreat is capital reallocation, moving resources from a losing position to a better one, not an admission of defeat.

steps.description: Capture the current commitment, its goal, and the resources tied up in it. You can only define retreat triggers against a clearly stated commitment and a clear measure of the resources at stake.

inputs.name: commitment-description
inputs.desc: The project, market, or bet you are committed to

inputs.name: stated-goal
inputs.desc: What the commitment is meant to achieve

inputs.name: committed-resources
inputs.desc: The money, people, and time currently tied up

outputs.name: commitment-profile
outputs.desc: The commitment and its goal stated clearly

outputs.name: resource-ledger
outputs.desc: The resources tied up and their rough value

process: State the commitment and the goal it is meant to reach, in plain terms.
List the resources tied up: money, people, time, and attention.
Estimate the rough value of those resources if they were free to use elsewhere.
Keep this factual. Triggers and judgments come in the next steps.

steps.description: Define retreat triggers in advance, while you can still think clearly. A trigger is a specific, observable condition that, once met, means it is time to pull back. Defining them now beats deciding under sunk-cost pressure later.

inputs.name: commitment-profile
inputs.desc: The commitment and its goal stated clearly

inputs.name: resource-ledger
inputs.desc: The resources tied up and their rough value

outputs.name: retreat-triggers
outputs.desc: The named conditions that would signal retreat

outputs.name: trigger-thresholds
outputs.desc: The measurable threshold for each trigger

process: Decide the conditions, set now, under which you would pull back from this commitment.
Make each trigger specific and observable, not a vague feeling that things are going badly.
Set a measurable threshold for each trigger so there is no arguing later about whether it fired.
Write them down now. Triggers defined under pressure get bent to protect the commitment.

steps.description: Define the opportunity-cost trigger: the point where the expected gain from continuing is less than what the same resources would earn elsewhere. Continuing past this point destroys value even if the commitment is not failing outright.

inputs.name: resource-ledger
inputs.desc: The resources tied up and their rough value

inputs.name: retreat-triggers
inputs.desc: The named conditions that would signal retreat

outputs.name: opportunity-cost-trigger
outputs.desc: The threshold where continuing costs more than it returns

outputs.name: alternative-use-estimate
outputs.desc: The best estimated return on the resources elsewhere

process: Estimate the expected gain from continuing the commitment as it stands.
Estimate the best return the same resources could earn in their next-best use.
Set the trigger at the point where continuing returns less than the alternative.
Record the alternative-use estimate so the comparison can be rechecked over time.

steps.description: Define the permanent-change trigger: the point where the conditions that made the commitment sensible have changed for good. A temporary setback is worth pushing through; a permanent change is not.

inputs.name: commitment-profile
inputs.desc: The commitment and its goal stated clearly

inputs.name: retreat-triggers
inputs.desc: The named conditions that would signal retreat

outputs.name: permanent-change-trigger
outputs.desc: The condition signaling a permanent shift against the commitment

outputs.name: change-indicators
outputs.desc: The observable signs that the shift is permanent, not temporary

process: Name the conditions the commitment depends on: a market need, a technology, a rule, a cost.
For each, define what a permanent adverse change would look like, not just a dip.
List the observable signs that would tell a permanent change from a temporary one.
Set the trigger to fire on permanent change, and resist firing it on normal volatility.

steps.description: Define the reallocation trigger: the point where the resources would produce a clear multiple of their current return if moved to a specific better use. This reframes retreat as moving capital to where it works hardest.

inputs.name: resource-ledger
inputs.desc: The resources tied up and their rough value

inputs.name: alternative-use-estimate
inputs.desc: The best estimated return on the resources elsewhere

outputs.name: reallocation-trigger
outputs.desc: The multiple at which moving resources is clearly worth it

outputs.name: reallocation-targets
outputs.desc: The specific better uses the resources would move to

process: Identify specific alternative uses that would clearly outperform the current commitment.
Estimate the multiple each alternative would return versus staying the course.
Set the trigger at a multiple high enough to cover the cost and disruption of moving.
Name the concrete targets so retreat has somewhere to send the resources.

steps.description: Set up monitoring so a triggered condition is actually noticed and acted on. A trigger nobody watches is useless, and sunk-cost pressure is strongest exactly when a trigger quietly fires.

inputs.name: opportunity-cost-trigger
inputs.desc: The threshold where continuing costs more than it returns

inputs.name: permanent-change-trigger
inputs.desc: The condition signaling a permanent shift against the commitment

inputs.name: reallocation-trigger
inputs.desc: The multiple at which moving resources is clearly worth it

outputs.name: monitoring-plan
outputs.desc: How and how often each trigger is checked

outputs.name: review-cadence
outputs.desc: The schedule and owner for trigger reviews

process: For each trigger, define the signal to watch and where it is measured.
Set a review cadence frequent enough to catch a trigger before heavy new losses pile up.
Assign an owner for each review, since an unwatched trigger never fires in practice.
Plan to pre-commit the response so the review is about facts, not relitigating the decision.

steps.description: Write the playbook for executing the retreat once a trigger fires: how to pull back in an orderly way and move the freed resources to their better use. A clean retreat keeps capital; a messy one burns it on the way out.

inputs.name: monitoring-plan
inputs.desc: How and how often each trigger is checked

inputs.name: reallocation-targets
inputs.desc: The specific better uses the resources would move to

outputs.name: retreat-playbook
outputs.desc: The ordered steps to pull back cleanly when a trigger fires

outputs.name: reallocation-schedule
outputs.desc: The plan to move freed resources to their targets

process: Write the ordered steps to wind down the commitment without wasting what can be recovered.
Cover obligations, communication, and what to preserve for reuse.
Schedule the move of freed resources to the reallocation targets so they do not sit idle.
Frame the retreat as reallocation of capital to a better use, and brief it that way.

description: Design a product that improves as more people use it. Identify the user-to-user interaction that creates value, make it the core of the product rather than a feature, solve the cold start problem, and set a metric that proves engagement per user rises as the user count grows. A real network effect is the hardest position for a rival to copy.

steps.description: Capture the product and the ways users could interact with each other. A network effect lives in a user-to-user interaction, so the first job is to find the candidate interactions worth examining.

inputs.name: product-description
inputs.desc: What the product does and for whom

inputs.name: user-types
inputs.desc: The kinds of users the product serves

inputs.name: current-value-source
inputs.desc: Where the product's value comes from today

outputs.name: product-profile
outputs.desc: A profile of the product and its users

outputs.name: interaction-candidates
outputs.desc: The user-to-user interactions that could create value

process: Describe the product and the kinds of users it serves.
List the ways users could interact: sharing, transacting, contributing, matching, communicating.
Note whether today's value comes from the product itself or from other users.
Collect the interaction candidates without judging them yet.

steps.description: Identify the one user-to-user interaction that most creates value as more users join. Most products have many possible interactions but one that truly drives the network effect. Find that one.

inputs.name: product-profile
inputs.desc: A profile of the product and its users

inputs.name: interaction-candidates
inputs.desc: The user-to-user interactions that could create value

outputs.name: core-interaction
outputs.desc: The single interaction that drives the network effect

outputs.name: value-mechanism
outputs.desc: How that interaction turns more users into more value per user

process: For each candidate interaction, ask whether it makes the product better for a user when more users join.
Keep the interactions that pass and discard the rest.
Pick the single interaction with the strongest link between more users and more value per user.
Describe the mechanism: exactly how added users raise the value each user gets.

steps.description: Make the value interaction the core of the product, not a side feature. Network effects fade when the interaction that drives them is buried behind features that give the same value without any other users.

inputs.name: core-interaction
inputs.desc: The single interaction that drives the network effect

inputs.name: value-mechanism
inputs.desc: How that interaction turns more users into more value per user

outputs.name: core-design
outputs.desc: The product reshaped around the core interaction

outputs.name: feature-demotions
outputs.desc: The features to demote or cut so they do not undercut the network

process: Redesign the main flow so the core interaction is the first and central thing a user does.
Identify features that deliver value without needing other users and may blunt the network effect.
Demote or cut those features so they do not compete with the network as the source of value.
Confirm a new user quickly reaches the core interaction rather than a single-user dead end.

steps.description: Solve the cold start problem: a network-effect product has little value before the network exists, so early users need a reason to show up first. Without a cold start answer, the network effect never gets to begin.

inputs.name: core-interaction
inputs.desc: The single interaction that drives the network effect

inputs.name: product-profile
inputs.desc: A profile of the product and its users

outputs.name: cold-start-plan
outputs.desc: How to give early users value before the network exists

outputs.name: single-player-value
outputs.desc: The standalone value that holds users until the network forms

process: Accept that early users arrive before the network gives much value.
Design standalone, single-user value that is worth using even with nobody else there.
Pick a narrow first segment where even a small network is dense enough to feel alive.
Plan the path from single-user value to the network kicking in as users accumulate.

steps.description: Map which type of network effect applies: direct, indirect, data, or social. The type decides how the effect scales, how defensible it is, and where it can be attacked by a rival.

inputs.name: core-interaction
inputs.desc: The single interaction that drives the network effect

inputs.name: value-mechanism
inputs.desc: How that interaction turns more users into more value per user

outputs.name: network-effect-type
outputs.desc: The type of network effect at work

outputs.name: defensibility-note
outputs.desc: How defensible that type is and its weak points

process: Classify the effect: direct same-side, indirect cross-side, data-driven, or social.
Note how the effect scales for that type and whether it stays local or goes global.
Name the weak points of that type, such as multi-homing or local networks a rival can beat city by city.
Record how defensible the effect is once it takes hold.

steps.description: Design the metric that proves the network effect is real: engagement per user should rise as the total user count grows. If each user engages the same or less as the network grows, there is no real network effect, only growth.

inputs.name: core-interaction
inputs.desc: The single interaction that drives the network effect

inputs.name: network-effect-type
inputs.desc: The type of network effect at work

outputs.name: engagement-metric
outputs.desc: The metric linking engagement per user to total user count

outputs.name: measurement-plan
outputs.desc: How and when the metric is tracked

process: Define engagement per user in terms of the core interaction, not vanity activity.
Set the key test: does engagement per user rise as the total user count grows?
Plan to track the metric over time and across cohorts of different network sizes.
Decide the reading that would disprove the network effect, so the metric can fail honestly.

steps.description: Monitor whether the network effect is real and strengthening over time, and set the rule for when to push growth harder. A network effect that is not strengthening is a cost center dressed up as a moat.

inputs.name: engagement-metric
inputs.desc: The metric linking engagement per user to total user count

inputs.name: cold-start-plan
inputs.desc: How to give early users value before the network exists

outputs.name: network-health-dashboard
outputs.desc: The ongoing view of network-effect health

outputs.name: scaling-decision-rule
outputs.desc: The rule for when to invest harder in growth

process: Track the engagement metric alongside user count to watch the effect strengthen or stall.
Watch the first segment from the cold start plan to confirm the effect holds as it widens.
Set the rule: push growth hard only once engagement per user clearly rises with scale.
Flag a stalling effect early, since scaling a weak network effect just raises cost.
